title: 3-Read Friday #10: Homework, Highlighting, and Interior Angles
author: Barton, Craig
summary: After a summer gap, issue ten returns with three research-grounded posts on established classroom debates. Barton opens with Michael Pershan's deep-dive into whether homework is worth assigning at all, noting how widely homework policy varies between the schools he visits and highlighting Pershan's findings on the quality and duration of assignments. He then covers Andrew Watson's review of a 2022 meta-analysis on highlighting, which challenges Barton's own "go-to advice" to highlight keywords in wordy maths problems — the research suggests this is likely wasted effort for younger students who don't yet know which words matter. He closes with the second instalment of Paul Rowlandson's interior-and-exterior-angles series, praising not just the maths content but Rowlandson's transferable planning process of teaching, reflecting, adapting, and re-teaching. All three items are grounded in classroom research and instructional technique, keeping the issue in Learning & Curriculum.
points: Barton flags that Pershan's research-based deep dive into homework specifically examines quality and duration, not just whether to assign it at all.
He admits his own long-standing advice to "highlight the keywords" is undercut by the meta-analysis Watson reviews, since younger students don't reliably know which words are worth highlighting.
He generalizes Rowlandson's angles-specific planning process — teach, reflect, adapt, re-teach — as a transferable model applicable to any topic in any subject.
quotes: The schools I visit often have radically different homework policies. Some assign it all online, others use worksheets. Some set homework twice a week, others set none at all.
In this post, Michael Pershan takes a deep-dive, and comes out with some practical findings, particularly about the quality and duration of homework.

Andrew Watson reviews a 2022 meta-analysis into the potential benefits and pitfalls of highlighting to suggest that my advice is likely to be a waste of time for younger students as they do not know which words to highlight.
But it is not all doom and gloom. The meta-analysis has some really useful, practical suggestions, such as modelling good highlighting and contrasting this with examples of bad highlighting.

But the principles Paul employs in terms of planning - reflecting how he has always taught something, experimenting with a new approach, reflecting on how it went and adapting accordingly - can be applied to any topic in any subject.
